title: HILLFORT
description: On the summit of Mallabeny Hill, on the N side of the Clogher Valley, with superb views all round. The hillfort is defined by a well preserved scarp which encircles the summit of the hill, creating an oval enclosure 170m NNW/ SSE x 140m SSW-NNE. The scarp varies 1-1.75m high & is surmounted by a bank 3.3m wide & 0.3m above a shallow inner ditch which is 3m wide & at best 0.7m deep. The interior is naturally domed but there is no evidence for internal structure or an entrance.

title: HILLFORT
description: On top of a hill with excellent views. The site is impressive, although some 52m of the N extent have been removed, where the bank & ditch would have been situated. The site, 71m E-W diam., stands proud of the field surface & is surrounded by an arc of waterlogged ditch running round the outside of the bank, which varies in height. At WSW, the bank is 1.25m above the interior, 5.4m wide & 2.35m above the ditch, which is 1.4m wide & 1m deep. The interior gradually slopes to N. See SM7 for further details. An archaeological evaluation was carried out on a proposed development site NE of the hillfort. Two test trenches were excavated across the development area. No artefacts or features of archaeological significance were uncovered [SOC 20/09/04].

title: Breiddin Hillfort;Breidden Hillfort
description: The Breiddin Hillfort (the spelling preferred in archaeological literature) enclosure is formed on the summit of an isolated and abrupt north-east to south-west orientated ridge, and is approximately 1,150m long and at most 250m across. It is defined by two or three widely spaced stone-revetted ramparts on the south-eastern side, with a centrally placed entrance, elsewhere defined by precipitous slopes. Excavations between 1933-5 and between 1969 and 1976 indicated an enclosure occupation sequence extending from the seventh century BC to the fourth century AD, with the ramparts substantially intact at the latter period (St John O'Neil 1937; Musson 1991). Examination of environmental evidence from the Buckbean Pond upon the summit indicates seasonal occupation of an extensive, rather than an intensive nature (Buckland et al. 2001). There is a lesser defended enclosure, with an associated field system approximately 270m to the south-east (NPRN 94037).  The Breiddin is one of the supposed sites of the battle fought between the British king Caratacas and the Roman general Ostorius Scapula in A.D.50.  The site has been partially destroyed by quarrying, and Rodney's Pillar (NPRN 32922) crowns the enclosed area.  Sources: St John O'Neil 1937 (AC 92), 86-128;                   Musson 1991 'The Breiddin Hillfort' CBA Research Report 76;                   Buckland et al. 2001 (Ant. J. 81), 51-76.  RCAHMW, October 2006.

title: SMALL HILLFORT
description: On top of a steep, rocky outcrop with magnificent views all round, this site remains as a large stone enclosure, approx. 60m diam., as shown on the OS maps. The walls are tumbled, varying 2-4m in width and up to 1m high in places. In the SE corner are the footings of a round house, set against the cashel wall. It is 5m diam.,  with walls approx. 0.7m wide & 1 or 2 courses high. Just outside the wall, by the house, a pathway of stones 1.5m wide & 5m long leads to a roughly circular area approx. 4m in diam., also paved with stones. Also just beside the house is a sunken area in the outer walling, possibly a collapsed souterrain [RR, 2001]. The site remains as described above. An annexe earthwork at W indentified from an AP could not be clearly translated on the ground.

title: Penybanc Hillfort
description: Oval, univallate hillfort first identified from vertical aerial photographs (RAF 548/488 frame 4038). The site occupies a prominent rounded hilltop at 206m OD which overlooks the steep valley of the River Severn on the south side. The hillfort is approximately 60m x 30m, aligned NE/SW. The principal defences are on the NE and E sides where a rampart defends the level approach to the hillfort. On the SW side the slopes are precipitous and few artificial defences were required apart from a slight scarping of the hillslope.  The site has not been visited on the ground but has been observed from nearby roads.  T Driver. 9th August 2004.

title: Possible Contour hillfort
description: Indentified from analysis of LiDAR and investigation of the former Episcopal Manor Landscape round the manor at the Abbacy. This is a large ovalinear enclosure set atop a drumlin with good commanding views in all directions, particularly out over Strangford Lough, toward the motte and bailey at Ardkeen, and over the manorial landscape of the Abbacy. It is estimated to measure approx. 200m N-S x up to 125m E-W, and in the northern part seems to follow the contour line shown on the 3rd edition Ordnance Survey map. The northern apex of the enclosure is most discernible on the ground. While visible as a slight depression at some other locations here there is a more discernible rise upward to the interior. The interior is the natural character of the hilltop. A hedge boundary runs east-west across the site. The ground is lower on the south side of this hedge boundary as a result of a lane having traversed this site, this feature being depicted on earlier ordnance survey map editions. It is possible that this feature is a contour hillfort

title: Maesydderwen Plantation Hillfort;Carreg Cegyn Hillfort
description: Iron Age hillfort comprising an upper oval, univallate, summit enclosure measuring 115m x 67m, overlying to the west part of a univallate oval enclosure, later annex or earlier hillfort 64m x 54m. The upper enclosure has 70m of a scree-built rampart and surviving gateway on the south side, recorded during RCAHMW aerial reconnaissance on 28th March 2012. This has parallels with Y Gaer Fawr, the hillfort on Garn Goch (NPRN 100866) to the east. The Dyfed Archaeological Trust visited the site in March 2008 (PRN 914) but apparently only recorded the low earthworks of the enclosure to the west of the summit fort. No mention is made of the scree-built rampart above. The whole encloses around 1.5 hectares, and is damaged by quarrying on the south side and obscured by woodland vegetation on the north side. The plan of the site is only clarified on LiDAR data.  T. Driver, RCAHMW, May 2015

title: Beacon Ring Hillfort; Caer Digoll Hillfort
description:
Oval univallate hillfort some 200m n-s by 170m e-w. Simple entrance at s and possible modern gap at n. Sited on highest point of n-s ridge (Long Mountain). Interior afforested in 1953. See also PRN 135 (round barrow sited within hillfort) and PRN 5620 (stone hammer find from surface).

The hillfort appears in a number of early myths and legends. One of the earliest of these is in the 9th- or 10th-century saga known as Canu Llywarch Hen (The song of Llywarch the Old), in a passage about hostilities in the 7th century between the British prince Cadwallon and Edwin, the Anglo-Saxon, king of Northumbria. Beacon Ring is described, somewhat poetically, as the lluest or camp of Cadwallon where he stayed for seven months, carrying out seven skirmishes daily.

A poem by Llywarch Hen states
"Lluent Cadwallawn glodrydd
Yn ngwarthas Digoll Vynydd"
[The army of the illustrious Cadwallawn
Encamped on Mount Digoll] (Hywel George, pers. comm. 2010)

title: Dinas Hillfort
description: Dinas hillfort is a strongly sited hillfort at 385m above sea level, which occupies a narrow ridge with very steep slopes on the west and east sides. The hillfort overlooks the upper Rheidol on the east side, and the tributary at the foot of the west side of the ridge is also deeply cut. Access to the summit is easiest from the south side, where one ascends from the more gradual terrain and meadow land flanking the Rheidol at Ponterwyd.     The hillfort is pear-shaped, 107m N/S by 51m E/W. Hogg (Cardiganshire County History 1994, 270) described the rampart as `'a stony bank, about 5.5m wide and just over a metre high externally.'. It appears to have been quarried from broad internal quarry ditches on the north and south sides. On the west the rampart partly incorporates the outcropping rock on the summit. The original entrance, an unelaborated gap, is centrally placed in the rampart on the south side and commands panoramic views to the south.      Hogg (ibid.) records one certain house platform and three possible; the certain platform lies towards the centre of the fort, but there is a second on the south side overlooking the main gate, and possibly two others on the north side. However, the northern part of the interior has been confused by digging, possibly from mining work in more recent decades. An internal subdivision, a low bank and ditch, cuts across the centre of the fort and may be an original feature. Visited on 9th January 2000.  A possible cist burial has been reported from the interior (?) of the enclosure (Nprn402234).  A platform, thought to represent a hut circle, is known some 450m to the south.  T Driver, RCAHMW, 15 September 2004.

title: Gaer Hillfort
description:
Multivallate contour fort with wide rampart interspace on north and east, possibly of two periods. Inner enclosure inturn and annex to east. Outer rampart possible inturn to east and outwork to west.

The Gaer is a multivallate fort, occupying the western portion of a ridge with its defences
following the contours. Cwm Cefu y Gaer hillfort lies a short distance away to the east. Conventionally this would be termed a multiple enclosure or widespaced-ramparted hillfort. The main enclosure has an inturned entrance on the north-east and beyond this are the incomplete remains of an outer enclosure or annexe. Surrounding both are the earthworks of a larger enclosure again incomplete, but with indications of a counterscarp along part of the western side and the incipient traces of an inturned entrance at the extreme north-east.

title: Afon Tarell Hillfort; Waenfaeog hillfort
description:
PROMONTORY FORT WITH DOUBLE RAMPARTS ISOLATING AN AREA OF SOME 0.75 HEC AND PROTECTION FROM STEEP NATURAL SLOPES ON NW. ORIGINAL ENTRANCE PROB IN E. MODERN TRACKWAY IN NW PART OF INTERIOR EMERGING AT SE.

Inland promontory fort situated on 2 connecting spurs of land overlooking the Afon Tarell. It is defended by steep natural slopes on its N, E and W sides, and by 3 lines of artificial ramparts with outer ditches on the SE. Ramparts average 2m in height and cut off the neck of the promontory. Its entrance probably lay on the E side where the inner and outer ramparts stop short of the natural slope. It is possible that a level platform at the E end of the middle rampart could have served as the base of a gatehouse. Good potential for surviving internal features. Hillfort forms part of an unusually complete Iron Age landscape (close to 4 other hillforts). Scheduled 12/10/98 (Cadw 1998).

title: Tilberthwaite Hillfort
description:
Site of a possible hillfort (a hilltop enclosure bounded by one or more substantial banks, ramparts and ditches-although this one is naturally defensible and needs no ramparts) of unknown date.

Occupation floors recorded at Tilberthwaite on a site which is inferred to have been a hillfort, possibly of 12th century origin-the name "Tillesburc" occurs in a document of 1157-63. The site is naturally defensible and needs no ramparts to make it a stronghold. Several of the rock hollows were excavated and found to contain a 2 in thick stratum of disturbed whitish grey sandy clay in which there are small flakes of stone and fragments of charcoal. This level underlies 8 in of black vegetable soil and overlies 4 in of dark grey sandy clay. No pottery or relics were found. See the Report of Congress of Archaeological Societies for 1923 (S912 p. 38). See the 1923 volume of C&WAAS (S2108 p. 138-141). According to OS the remains resemble earlier hut floors of the Mardale Castle Crag and possibly the Cater rock-huts of Peel Island (S1361). Site recorded within The National Trust Sites and Monuments Record as a a possible Medieval fort is situated on a high ridge at Low Coppice (S2873). The site might be that of the place "Tillesbure" which is recorded within a document dated between 1157 and 1163 (S2925). The place-name itself is of historic interest and derives from a Scandinavian root (S2926). Fieldwork by The National Trust could not locate the site (R Maxwell, 15.03.1994, S2922)

title: Llwynrhidaf Hillfort
description:
Remains of banks on north and west side of hill but much damaged by quarrying. Possible univallate enclosure around natural outcrop (CPAT 1981).


CPAT: the available RAF APs showed nothing of interest. The postulated site, is located on a local summit (302m 00), 460m north-east of Twyn Llechfaen hillfort (PRN 620), and south-east of Llwynrhydaf Farm. There are a number of relict field boundaries visible, together with a holloway track that traverses the area of improved pasture, east to west. The banks referred to in the previous site report are formed from post-medieval quarry spoil, the 'ditches' being surface quarry rakes.
There is a large amount of quarry stone and field clearance littering the northern extent ofthe site.
Consequently, no evidence for an enclosure was recorded (CPAT Defended Enclosures in Brecknock Project, 2007).

title: LEWESDON HILLFORT
description: A large univallate hillfort on the top of a narrow hill. The hillfort is defended on its south western and south eastern sides by a precipitous scarp. Along the northern side where the slope is less steep there are traces of an infilled ditch about 7 metres below the level of the interior which covers an area of about 1.2ha. At the western and southern end the hillfort is approached across narrow ridges which create natural causeways. At the western end, crossing the ridge, there is a slight ditch, 2.5 metres wide and 0.5 metres deep, with traces of an outer bank, 4 metres wide and up to 0.5 metres high. Inside the enclosure there are traces of a bank, up to 0.5 metres high, running along the edge of the scarp which may be the remains of an inner rampart. Similarly at the southern end the slope levels off suggesting an infilled ditch with a counterscarp bank which crosses the ridge. The line of the ditch continues as a ledge along the south western scarp for about 80 metres. There is a possible internal rampart cutting across the ridge 4 metres wide and up to 0.8 metres high at this end. The interior of the hillfort has been disturbed by gravel digging and timber removal. Scheduled.

title: Dumpdon Hillfort
description:
Dumpdon Camp on the summit of Dumpdon Hill is a triangular Iron Age hill-fort, the narrowest part of the camp pointing south and the broad top running NE-SW. At the northern end, where the approach is relatively easy, there is a double bank and double ditch, approximately 15.24m apart. At its highest point, the inner defences here are 1.83m high on the interior side, with a 4.3m perpendicular fall on the exterior side. The ditch, which is 0.6m deep, is surrounded by an outer bank 1.2m high with an escarpment of 4.3m and a ditch of 1.7m deep. On the naturally precipitous slopes of the south eastern and south western sides, the defences were increased by the construction of a double bank and single ditch. The inner bank is now a narrow platform divided into two terraces, only the lower one has the imperfect remains of an outer rampart which rises to 1.83m high at the southern point on the edge of the natural descent. At the entrance, which is on the north-eastern side, the inner and outer ramparts inflect and are carried approximately 30m into the interior of the camp, forming a passage in which any enemy would be exposed to cross fire. Beneath the entrance are strategically-placed terraced earthworks, which would restrict direct access. Part of the earthwork, although well-preserved, has been disturbed in places by ploughing which occurred in the area within the fort, and by mechanical excavations resulting from interest created in the site by local dowsers.
The banks and other earthwork defences of Dumpdon Hill survive as quite impressive remains, with largely undamaged stratification. They are, however, not easily appreciated by the public due to dense gorse and bracken growth. There are also some small areas of erosion where footpaths come straight over the banks.
In the interior of the hill-fort, a beech plantation, which was probably in existance in 1840, dominates the southern third (underplanted in 1967). Immediately to the north of the present plantation is a small triangular area of land, which appears not to have been planted, and has certainly not been ploughed. The remainder of the interior has been ploughed and immediately adjacent to the entrance has been severely damaged by mechanical excavations. (NT Archaeological Survey July 1984)
Todd believes that the defences were begun on the N side where there is a double rampart and that the lesser defences on the E and W sides and 'untidy dumps' on the W side indicate that the defences were never completed. Limited (unpublished) excavations and examination where trees had been uprooted in 1990 found no archaeological features also leading Todd to believe that the site was never completed or occupied. He speculates that it could predate and was superseded by the construction of Hembury, Peyhembuery a few miles to the West (DAS/NT leaflet 1994).
A trianulation point on a mound in the centre of the hillfort (100096) and another mound adjacent to the SW defence (100209) have been suggested as later beacon sites.
Hutchinson and the VCH provide plans. A new plan was drawn by the OS in 1982. Woollcombe (1836 in Manuscript) mentions the boundary across the interior of the hillfort. An air photo by D. Wayne in July 1990 shows an ovoid enclosure type mark within the hillfort, but origin unclear - copy held by County SMR. (Devon County SMR ST10SE-016)

title: Garth Hillfort
description:
An arcuate bank (12m long) and external ditch (29m long) forming the south-east segment of the enclosure. A possible entrance on the west. Apparently a hillfort despite assertions to contrary by Crampton (Crampton, C B, 1966b; Crampton, C B, 1967).

As previously described. (CPAT Tir Gofal assessment, 2003)

title: Breiddin hillfort
description:
Multivallate hillfort with two and three ramparts on south-east site. Excavated in 1933-35 and in 1969-75 revealing possible mesolithic, late neolithic, early bronze age, iron age, late Roman and possible dark age activity.

Summary of Buckbean pond environmental project in Musson, C R, Smith, A G & Girling, M 1984, 71

Final excavation report (Musson, C R et al 1991).

Main areas of excavation:
RAMPARTS: evidence for pre-rampart deposits (Mesolithic/Neolithic/Early Bronze Age); late Bronze Age rampart of paired postholes with a core of stone and soil and a rear kerb; Iron Age - lower core of stones and soil, upper core of voided scree, front facing of large boulders and scree and rear facing of variable material (no internal timbering).
